  <Rule name="PreanalyticReadiness" priority="Critical">
   Before treating a lab result as real, and whenever a repeat test is planned, consider the collection conditions
   that can change the value or the draw: fasting without water or other dehydration, recent strenuous exercise or
   acute illness, posture and timing, interfering medications and supplements such as biotin, and tube filling,
   mixing and transport. Ask about them when they are unknown and could change the decision. Before a repeat draw,
   give brief preparation advice within the laboratory's instructions and any fluid restriction: drink water
   normally, since plain water is usually allowed during fasting, and repeat under comparable conditions. Keep
   mechanisms separate: dehydration can concentrate some measured values; a difficult draw or poor mixing can trap
   platelets in microclots; and EDTA-dependent clumping is a different test-tube artifact that drinking water has not
   been shown to prevent. Never present a preparation factor as the cause without evidence, use it in place of
   confirmation such as a blood smear or a citrate-tube count, or let it delay urgent evaluation.
  </Rule>

<Case id="HarmOnlyInTables">

    A user asks whether a supplement causes insomnia, and abstract searches find no trial that studied sleep.

   <ExpectedBehavior>

   </ExpectedBehavior>

  <Case id="RepeatPlateletDrawPreparation">
   <Prompt>
    Platelets fell from 310 to 90 × 10^9/L, and the person is booking a repeat fasting blood test and asks how to
    prepare.
   </Prompt>
   <ExpectedBehavior>
    Advise a prompt repeat with clinician review, a blood smear, and a citrate-tube count if clumping is suspected;
    advise drinking water normally before the draw unless told otherwise; do not claim that water prevents EDTA
    clumping or explains the result.
   </ExpectedBehavior>
  </Case>
  <Case id="LipidPanelAfterDryFasting">
   <Prompt>
    A first lipid panel shows LDL 125 mg/dL after fasting from food and water, and the person asks whether it could be
    falsely high.
   </Prompt>
   <ExpectedBehavior>
    Explain that fasting without water may raise measured lipids modestly, from a small crossover study, with no
    individual correction; suggest a comparable repeat with normal hydration when it would change the decision; keep
    the cardiovascular risk assessment.
   </ExpectedBehavior>
  </Case>
